intro: Three low notes, A–G♯–C♯, begin the Prelude that followed Rachmaninoff into almost every recital hall. He plays it here for Edison in 1919; the quiet opening chords return with enough notes to need four staves.

sections.label: A · Three low notes, quiet chords
B · Agitato: the triplets begin
sections.mNote: A descending melody inside continuous triplets

sections.label: A′ · The chords fill four staves
sections.mNote: Tempo primo; both hands double the opening chords

sections.label: Coda · Chords over a low C♯
sections.mNote: The bass holds C♯ while the upper chords change

cues.title: Three notes, then a whisper
cues.text: A–G♯–C♯, struck in low octaves. The answering chords are marked ppp, three degrees of quiet against the opening’s ff. The same three bass notes return beneath them, sounding through the spaces in the right hand.
cues.evidence: Mutopia edition, after Bosworth and Universal Edition, opening through bar 3: octave motto and ppp answering chords. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/RachmaninoffS/O3/rach-prelude-op3-no2/rach-prelude-op3-no2-a4.pdf
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: An encore for life
cues.text: In 1893 Gutheil pays the nineteen-year-old Rachmaninoff forty roubles for the Prelude. The piece travels around the world. Years later, audiences still refuse to let him leave the platform without playing it.
cues.evidence: Robert Matthew-Walker’s notes for Hyperion CDA66081 give the fee, February 1893 publication and audiences’ demands for the Prelude as an encore. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6690_66081

cues.title: Triplets carry the melody
cues.text: Agitato: the right hand begins its running triplets over a held low C♯. Inside them, a melody descends by semitones, E–D♯–D♮–C♯. The bass is still; the upper notes cannot settle.
cues.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 14–16: Agitato, C♯ bass and descending chromatic melody within the triplets.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Four staves, two hands
cues.text: The opening chords return at Tempo primo, marked fff pesante — very loud and heavy. Rachmaninoff writes them on four staves, two for each hand. The little pianissimo answer now stretches across the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 45–54: Tempo primo, fff pesante and four-stave piano notation.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: C♯ beneath the changing chords
cues.text: The bass settles on C♯ and stays there. Above it, the chords continue to shift by semitones, separated now by rests. The final C♯ minor chord is marked ppp, as quiet as the answer near the beginning.
cues.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 55–61: C♯ pedal, changing upper harmonies and final ppp C♯ minor chord.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: A held bass beneath the triplets
transitions.from: A · Three low notes, quiet chords
transitions.how: The left hand repeats A–G♯ and lands on C♯. Above that held bass, Agitato sets the right hand moving in triplets, with E–D♯–D♮–C♯ descending through them. C♯ minor remains the home key; the long pauses between chords have gone.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 13–16; the established join corresponds to bar 14, marked Agitato.

transitions.title: The bass announces the return
transitions.to: A′ · The chords fill four staves
transitions.how: The running chords stop on two enormous bass notes, A and G♯. F♯ minor over A moves to a G♯ dominant seventh, then resolves into C♯ minor at Tempo primo. The bass has played the opening signal again; both hands answer with doubled chords, marked fff pesante.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 44–46; the established join corresponds to bar 45, Tempo primo.

transitions.title: The low C♯ stays
transitions.from: A′ · The chords fill four staves
transitions.to: Coda · Chords over a low C♯
transitions.how: A diminuendo brings the doubled chords down to mf. The bass reaches C♯ and repeats it while the hands play shorter, separated chords above. Their chromatic notes gradually clear, leaving a plain C♯ minor chord at ppp.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia edition, bars 53–61; the established coda join corresponds to bar 55.

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
